May the next generation catch a spark of that flame! It shone so brightly in the spirit and life of this faithful servant of the Most High God!”
2. One of the English newspapers has printed a fuller description of his character, and it is just as fair.
You may like it if I add the main points of this one too: —
“Every friend of true, living religion must have the character of this truly godly man [deeply] printed on their heart.

His body was weak [and delicate]. Even so, right up to the last day of his life, he kept preaching so often and so passionately that it seemed to be more than even the strongest person could naturally do.
He was called to do the work of a minister at an age when most young men are only starting to train for it. So he did not have time to get very far in learning the ancient languages.
But he more than made up for this with a lively and creative mind, with burning zeal, and with a powerful and very persuasive way of speaking.
In the pulpit he often found he had to “persuade people” by speaking of “the terror of the Lord.” Yet there was nothing gloomy about him. He was unusually cheerful, and also generous and kindhearted.
He was just as ready to help with people’s physical needs as with their spiritual needs when they came to him.
It should also be noted that he always urged his listeners to do every moral duty. He especially urged them to work hard at their jobs and to obey those in charge of them.

He worked incredibly hard at preaching in many different places, even in open fields. He did this to wake up the poorer people from the deepest carelessness and ignorance, so that they would begin to take religion seriously.
Because of this, and his other work, the name of GEORGE WHITEFIELD will be remembered with respect and honor for a long time.”
3. Everyone will readily agree that both of these accounts are true and fair—as far as they go.
But they hardly go beyond the outside of his character.
They show you the preacher. But they do not show you the man, the Christian, the saint of God.
May I add a little about this? I knew him personally for nearly forty years.
I know very well how hard it is to speak about such a delicate subject. It takes great wisdom to avoid both extremes and to say neither too little nor too much!
In fact, I know it is impossible to say anything at all—whether less or more—without some people blaming me for saying too little, and others for saying too much.
Some will honestly think I have said too little, and others that I have said too much.
But I will not let that worry me. I will say just what I know, in the presence of the One to whom we all must give an account.

4. We have already mentioned his zeal, which no one could match. We have mentioned how he never tired of working, how tender he was toward people who were suffering, and how generous he was to the poor.
But shouldn’t we also mention how deeply thankful he was to everyone God had used to do him good? He never stopped speaking about them with the greatest respect, right up to the day he died.
Shouldn’t we mention that his heart was open to the most generous and tender friendship?
I have often thought that this, more than anything else, was what made his character stand out.
How few people we have known with such a kind nature, with such big and overflowing love!
Wasn’t this the main reason why other people’s hearts were so wonderfully drawn to him and joined to his?
Can anything except love produce love?
This love shone in his very face. It breathed through all his words all the time, whether in public or in private.
Wasn’t it this love that flew from heart to heart, as fast and piercing as lightning? Wasn’t it this that gave such life to his sermons, his conversations, and his letters?
You yourselves are witnesses!
5. But away with the ugly twisting of this by people with dirty minds, who know no love except the earthly, physical kind!
At the same time, remember that he had the purest and most spotless modesty.
His work as a minister meant that he often had long talks with women as well as men, of every age and situation in life.
But the way he acted toward them was a living example of St. Paul’s advice to Timothy: “Appeal to the older women as mothers, and to the younger women as sisters, in all purity.”
6. His friendly spirit also fit well with how open and honest he was when he talked with people! And yet he was never rude on the one hand, and never sneaky [or pretending] on the other.
Wasn’t this openness both a result of his courage and fearlessness, and a proof of it?

With these as his armor, he was not afraid of anyone. He “spoke very plainly” to people of every rank and situation, high and low, rich and poor. His only goal was, “by making the truth clear, to win a place in every person’s conscience in the sight of God.”
7. He was not afraid of hard work or pain, any more than he was afraid of “what people [could] do to him.” He was just as

blocks.x: Patient in putting up with trouble as in doing good.

s: You could see this in how steadily he kept at whatever he took on for his Master’s sake.
Take just one example: the orphanage in Georgia. He started it and finished it, even though everything seemed to be against him.
In things that only concerned himself, he was easygoing and flexible.
In those cases he was “easy to reason with.” It was easy to convince him or to persuade him.
But in the things of God, or wherever his conscience was involved, no one could move him.
No one could talk him into changing even the smallest point, and no one could scare him into it either. His integrity was part of his whole character, and it guided everything he said and did.
In this he truly did

blocks.x:
Stand like a strong iron pillar,
And firm as a wall of bronze.

s: 8. Someone may ask what the foundation was for this integrity, or for his sincerity, courage, patience, and all his other good and lovely qualities. The answer is easy.

It was not that he was born with a good nature. It was not his great intelligence. It was not the power of his education. No, and it was not the advice of his friends. It was nothing else but faith in a Lord who bled for him, “faith that God Himself works in us.”
It was “a living hope of an inheritance that will never rot, never be stained, and never fade.”
It was “the love of God spread through his heart by the Holy Spirit, who was given to him.” That love filled his soul with tender, unselfish love for every human being.

This was the source of that flood of eloquence that often swept away everything in its path. This was the source of that amazing power to persuade, which even the most hardened sinners could not resist.
This was what often made him weep as if his “head were full of water, and his eyes a fountain of tears.”
This was what helped him pour out his soul in prayer in his own special way. His prayers were full and flowing at the same time, with such strength and variety in both thoughts and words.

9. I will finish this point by showing the great honor God gave His faithful servant. God let him announce His everlasting good news in so many different countries, to so many people, and with such a great effect on so many of their precious souls!
Since the time of the Apostles, have we ever read or heard of anyone who spread the good news of God’s grace over such a wide area, through so much of the inhabited world?
Have we ever read or heard of anyone who called so many thousands, even tens of thousands, of sinners to repent?
Above all, have we read or heard of anyone God has used so wonderfully to bring so many sinners “from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God”?
It is true that if we talked this way to people who live for pleasure, they would think we were speaking a foreign language.
But you understand the language of the country you are traveling to, where our dear friend has gone a little ahead of us.
III. But how can we gain something good from this solemn event that God has sent?
This is the third thing we need to think about.
The answer to this important question is easy. (May God write it in all our hearts!)
We do it by holding tightly to the great teachings he preached, and by soaking up his spirit.
1. So first, let us hold tightly to the great Bible teachings that he preached everywhere.
There are many teachings that are less essential. On these, even sincere children of God have disagreed for many centuries, and they still do. That is how weak human understanding is right now.
On these points we can think for ourselves and let others think for themselves. We can “agree to disagree.”

But at the same time, let us hold on firmly to the essentials of “the faith that was once handed down to the saints.” This champion of God insisted so strongly on these, at all times and in all places!
2. His most basic point was: “Give God all the credit for whatever is good in people.” And: “When it comes to salvation, lift Christ up as high as possible, and put people as low as possible.”
He and his friends at Oxford, the first people called Methodists, started out with this point.
Their great principle was this: by nature people have no power of their own, and nothing in them earns God’s favor.

They insisted that all the power to think, speak, or act rightly is in the Spirit of Christ and comes from Him. And everything that earns God’s favor is found only in the blood of Christ—not in people, no matter how far they have grown in grace.
That is what he and they taught. People have no power, until it is given to them from above, to do one good deed, to speak one good word, or even to have one good desire.
It is not enough to say that everyone is sick with sin. No, we are all “dead in our wrongdoing and sins.”
So it follows that all human beings are “by nature children under God’s anger.”
We are all “guilty before God,” and we deserve to die, both in this life and forever.
3. And we are all helpless, both against the power of sin and against its guilt.
“For who can make something clean out of something unclean?”
No one but the Almighty.
Who can raise people who are dead—spiritually dead in sin?
No one but the One who raised us up from the dust of the earth.
But why would He do this?
“Not on account of any right things we have done.”
“The dead cannot praise You, O Lord.” And they cannot do anything to earn being brought back to life.
So whatever God does, He does only for the sake of His dearly loved Son. “He was wounded because of our rebellion. He was bruised because of our evil.”
He Himself “bore” all “our sins in His own body on the wooden cross.”
He “was given up for our wrongs, and was raised again so that we could be declared right with God.”
So here is the only thing that earns every blessing we have or ever can have. This is especially true of our forgiveness, of God accepting us, and of our being fully and freely made right with Him.
But how do we come to have a share in what Christ has done and suffered?
“Not by our own deeds, so that nobody can brag.” We receive it by faith alone.
“We conclude,” says the Apostle, “that a person is made right with God by faith, without doing the works the law requires.”
And “to all who” in this way “receive Him, He gives the power to become sons of God—to those who believe in His name. They are born, not because a human being wanted it, but because of God.”
4. And “unless a person is” born again in this way, “he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
But everyone who is “born of the Spirit” in this way has “the kingdom of God inside them.”
Christ sets up His kingdom in their hearts: “right living, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.”
They have in them “the same mind that was in Christ Jesus.” This makes them able to “walk just as Christ walked.”
His Spirit, living in them, makes them holy in their hearts and also “holy in every part of their lives.”
But all of this is still a free gift, given because of Christ’s goodness and His blood. So there is always the same reason to remember: “Anyone who brags should brag about the Lord.”
5. You know very well that these are the basic teachings he insisted on everywhere.
And can’t they be summed up in two phrases: the new birth, and being made right with God by faith?
Let us insist on these teachings boldly, at all times and in all places. Those of us who are called to it should do so in public, and we should all do so in private whenever we get the chance.
Hold on tight to these good, old, unfashionable teachings, no matter how many people argue against them and insult them.
Keep going, my brothers and sisters, “in the name of the Lord, and in the power of His strength.”
Carefully and faithfully “keep safe what has been put in your care.” Know that “heaven and earth will pass away, but this truth will never pass away.”
6. But is it enough to hold tightly to his teachings, however pure they are?
Isn’t there something even more important than this? Isn’t it to soak up his spirit—to follow him in this, just as he followed Christ?
Without this, pure teaching would only make our judgment worse.
So this is the main thing: to copy his spirit.
We have to admit that in some ways we can only admire what we cannot copy. But in many other ways we can share in the same blessing, through the same free grace.

So remember how much you lack and how generous His love is. He “gives freely and does not scold.” Cry out to Him, the One who does everything in everyone, for some of the same precious faith, the same zeal and energy, the same tender heart, generosity, and deep, heartfelt mercy.
Wrestle with God in prayer for some of the same thankful, friendly, loving nature, the same openness, simplicity, and godly sincerity, and “love that does not pretend.”
Keep wrestling until the power from on high produces in you the same steady courage and patience. And above all, ask for the same unchanging integrity, because that is the crown of everything!
7. Was there any other fruit of God’s grace that he had in a special way? Was there something that he often and passionately grieved to see missing among God’s children?

Yes, there is one: catholic love. That is the sincere and tender love we owe to everyone we have reason to believe is a child of God by faith. In other words, it is love for everyone, in every church group, who “fears God and does right.”
He longed to see everyone who had “had a taste of God’s good word” have a truly catholic spirit. Many people often say that word, but few understand it, and even fewer have experienced it.
Who fits this description?
Who is the person with a catholic spirit?

It is someone who loves all who believe in the Lord Jesus, no matter what their opinions, their way of worship, or their church. He loves them as friends, as brothers and sisters in the Lord, as people who share with him in the kingdom of heaven now, and as fellow heirs of God’s eternal kingdom. He loves all who love God and people, who are glad to please God and afraid to offend Him, who are careful to stay away from evil, and who are eager to do good.

A person with a truly catholic spirit keeps all these people on his heart all the time. He cares for them more tenderly than words can say, and he truly wants what is best for them. So he never stops praying to God for them, and he also stands up for them in front of others. He speaks words of comfort to them, and with everything he says he works to make them stronger in God.
He helps them as much as he possibly can in everything, both spiritual and practical. He is ready to “spend and be spent” for them. Yes, he is ready “to lay down his life for his brothers.”
8. What a lovely character this is!
Every child of God should long for it!
So why is it so rarely found?
Why are there so few examples of it?
If we really have tasted God’s love, how can any of us rest until we have this love too?
Well, Satan has a clever trick. With it he convinces thousands of people that they can stop short of this love and still not be guilty.
I fear that many people here may be caught in this “snare of the devil,” where he has trapped them to do as he pleases.
“Oh yes,” someone says, “I have all this love for the people I believe are God’s children. But I will never believe that anyone who belongs to that awful church is a child of God!
Do you really think someone who holds such terrible opinions could be a child of God? Or someone who joins in such foolish and superstitious worship—maybe even idol worship?”
So we try to excuse one sin by adding a second one to it!
We excuse our own lack of love by blaming other people!
To cover up our own devilish attitude, we declare that our brothers and sisters are children of the devil!
Oh, watch out for this! And if you are already caught in this trap, get out of it as fast as you can!

Go and learn that truly catholic love that “is not reckless” or quick to judge. It is the love that “does not think evil,” that “believes and hopes all things.” It is the love that makes all the allowances for others that we want others to make for us!

Then we will recognize the grace of God in every person, whatever their opinion or way of worship. Then everyone who fears God will be close and dear to us, “with the deep, heartfelt love of Jesus Christ.”
9. Wasn’t this the spirit of our dear friend?
So why shouldn’t it be ours too?
O God of love, how long will Your people be a joke among unbelievers?
How long will they laugh at us and say, “Look how these Christians love one another!”
When will You take away our shame?
Will the sword go on destroying forever?
How long will it be before You tell Your people to turn back from “chasing after each other”?
Now, at least, “let all the people stop, and chase their brothers no more!”
But whatever other people do, my brothers and sisters, let all of us listen to the voice of this man who, though he is dead, still speaks!
Imagine that you hear him say, “Now, at least, follow my example, as I followed Christ!
Let brother “never again raise a sword against brother, and never learn war anymore!”
Instead, as God’s chosen people, put on hearts full of mercy, humble minds, brotherly kindness, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another in love.
You have spent enough time already on fighting, jealousy, and arguing, and on biting and tearing each other apart.
Praise God that you have not destroyed each other long ago!
From now on, hold on to the oneness that the Spirit gives, tied together with peace.”
10. O God, nothing is impossible for You!
You do whatever You please!
Oh, how we wish You would make the cloak of Your prophet, whom You have taken up to Yourself, fall on us who are left behind!
“Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?”
Let his spirit rest on these servants of Yours!
Show that You are the God who answers by sending fire!
Let the fire of Your love fall on every heart!
And because we love You, help us love one another with a “love that is stronger than death!”
Take away from us “all anger, rage, and bitterness, all shouting and hurtful talk!”
Let Your Spirit rest on us so that from this moment on we may be “kind to one another, gentle-hearted, forgiving each other, in the same way that God has forgiven us for Christ’s sake!”

1 Well done, servant of God!
Your great fight is over now;
The battle is fought, the race is won,
And you are crowned at last.
Everything your heart longed for
Is yours now in triumph;
The ministering choir has placed you
Close to your Redeemer’s heart.

2 In love that stooped down low,
He heard your constant prayer;
He called you to leave suddenly
For your full reward.
Your beautiful feet had shoes on,
Ready to bring the news of peace,
When mercy signed your soul’s release
And took you up to God.

3 With saints on thrones up high,
You now praise your Lord,
And still you cry, “Salvation to God!
Salvation to the Lamb!”
O happy, happy soul!
Filled with the joy of praise,
As long as endless ages roll,
You see your Savior’s face!

4 Set free from earth and pain,
Oh, when will we rise up
And all reign where Jesus is
With our friend who was taken up?
Come, Lord, come quickly!
And when we are made complete in You,
Bring Your longing servants home
To celebrate in triumph at Your feet!
